blocks.b:
Rickenbacker's own history calls the Electro String Instrument Corporation the first company founded for the sole purpose of creating and manufacturing fully electric musical instruments and amplifiers, and dates its first instruments to 1931.

The instrument was a lap steel. It was nicknamed the Frying Pan.

media.note: 정면 누끼. 후보: Wikimedia 'Flying Pan prototype (1931)' CC BY-SA 2.0 / 대안: 특허 Fig.1 도면(PD)

blocks.b:
George Beauchamp — pronounced Beechum — was a steel guitar player in Los Angeles in the 1920s who wanted a louder guitar.

He worked with the Dopyera brothers at National on metal-bodied resonator guitars. That partnership soured. John Dopyera left and formed the Dobro Corporation while keeping his National stock, and Beauchamp eventually left too.

media.note: National 트라이콘 리조네이터 기타 / 선택: 1930년대 하와이안 밴드 연주 아카이브 영상

blocks.b:
Beauchamp had been experimenting since about 1925. By 1930 he had a pickup built from two horseshoe magnets, with the strings passing over a coil fitted with six pole pieces, one under each string.

Rickenbacker's history records that it took "many months of trial and error."

media.note: 혼스슈 픽업 클로즈업 + 특허 Fig.2 단면도. 스크롤로 자석·코일·줄 레이어를 하나씩 켜는 연출
media.caption: The horseshoe pickup. The strings pass between the magnet arms, over a coil with six pole pieces.

blocks.b:
With the pickup working, Beauchamp called on Harry Watson, a skilled craftsman who had been National's factory superintendent, to make a wooden neck and body for it.

Watson carved it in several hours, using hand tools. The company's account describes the result as the first fully electric guitar, and says the nickname followed "for obvious reasons."

To manufacture it, Beauchamp enlisted Adolph Rickenbacker — Swiss-born, a highly skilled production engineer, and the owner of one of the largest deep-drawing presses on the West Coast, which had already made him a supplier of metal bodies to National.

The company was founded in Los Angeles in 1931 as Ro-Pat-In Corporation and soon renamed Electro String. Adolph became president, Beauchamp secretary-treasurer. Production began in a small rented shop at 6071 S. Western Avenue, next door to Rickenbacker's tool and die plant.

The instruments carried the Rickenbacker name because Adolph was related to the First World War flying ace Eddie Rickenbacker, and because it was easier to say than Beauchamp.

media.note: 초기 Electro String 로고 또는 1930년대 카탈로그 표지 / 공장 위치 그래픽(6071 S. Western Ave, LA)
media.caption: Rickenbacker Electro nameplate, Los Angeles.

blocks.b:
Beauchamp filed on 8 June 1932. The application stalled. By Rickenbacker's account the Patent Office did not know whether the Frying Pan was an electrical device or a musical instrument, and no patent category included both.

He refiled as a continuation on 2 June 1934. U.S. Patent 2,089,171 was granted on 10 August 1937, five years after the first filing.

The specification states one object as an instrument that "does not depend upon a sound board, resonance box, or the like in the production or propagation of the sound of the desired quality, whereby the body of the instrument may be of simple, inexpensive construction."

It describes strings whose "opposite ends are rigidly and unyieldingly connected to the rigid metallic body so that their major portions may have long periods of vibration with no dampening action due to the absorption of the vibrations by wooden body parts."

media.note: US2089171 1페이지 전문(PD, 고해상도 확보). 스크롤에 따라 도면 선이 그려지는 연출
media.caption: U.S. Patent 2,089,171, filed 1932, granted 1937.

blocks.b:
The production Frying Pan was cast aluminium rather than Watson's carved wood. The patent calls the body "a simple integral casting of metal, such as aluminum or the like."

It was offered in six- and seven-string versions, in 22½-inch and 25-inch scale lengths. Rickenbacker's history says the model remained available into the 1950s.

Aluminium expands under stage lights, and the necks went sharp as they warmed.

media.note: 알루미늄 바디·넥 디테일, 내부 신문지 샷 + 스펙 박스
media.caption: Stripped for service. Body and neck are a single aluminium casting.

blocks.b:
Six pole pieces sit under the strings, one for each, between the two arms of the magnet. The volume control is the only knob on the instrument.

The bridge is a plate screwed to the top of the casting. There is nothing inside the body for it to drive.

media.caption: Bridge plate, pickup, volume control and the output jack in the rim.

blocks.b: An original played and explained.

By 1940, after fifteen years in the fast lane, Beauchamp was frustrated and disenchanted with the instrument business, partly because of his deteriorating health. He sold his Electro String shares to Harold Kinney, the company's bookkeeper, to fund a fishing lure he had patented.

He died of a heart attack while deep-sea fishing. Rickenbacker records that his funeral procession was over two miles long.

Adolph Rickenbacker kept making instruments until 1953, when he and the other shareholders sold their interests to Francis C. Hall, who ran the Radio and Television Equipment Company and had been Leo Fender's exclusive distributor since 1946.

Rickenbacker treats that sale as the beginning of the modern company. Electro String still exists as the corporate entity; its name was changed to Rickenbacker International Corporation during a later series of mergers.

Gibson's own history frames the brief this way: by the time the company began work on its first electric guitar it had a forty-year tradition to uphold, and "the first Gibson electric had to be nothing less than the best electric guitar the world had ever seen."

media.note: 정면 누끼. 후보: 'Gibson Electro Spanish-150, Prototype Batch (1936), Museum of Making Music' CC BY-SA 2.0, 2448px

blocks.b:
In the spring of 1935 Gibson enlisted the musician Alvino Rey to help develop a prototype pickup with engineers at the Lyon & Healy company in Chicago. Later that year the research was moved in-house, where the Gibson employee Walter Fuller came up with the final design.

Gibson introduced the resulting hexagonal pickup on a lap steel model in late 1935.

media.note: 1935~36년 깁슨 칼라마주 공장 사진 또는 EH-150 랩스틸 이미지

blocks.b: The pickup was then installed on an f-hole archtop guitar, dubbed the ES-150 — ES for Electric Spanish — and the first one shipped from the Gibson factory in Kalamazoo, Michigan, on 20 May 1936.

Guy Hart had filed a patent on 8 February 1936. Its stated objects:

"First, to provide an electrically amplified stringed instrument embodying a body member which is substantially non-resonant and means for amplifying music produced thereon to any desired degree. Second, to provide an instrument of the class described, which is amplified solely due to the effect of variations in an air gap produced by the vibrating strings. Third, to provide an instrument of the type described, which is handsome in appearance."

The method: "I have designed the body of the instrument with a relatively thick wall of hard wood or of metal which is substantially lacking in the quality of resonance."

Gibson filed this and shipped a hollow archtop.

media.note: US2087106 Fig.1 (퍼블릭 도메인). 기타와 앰프가 케이블로 이어진 도면이라 '앰프가 있어야 완성되는 악기'라는 개념을 그대로 보여줌. 스크롤에 따라 선이 그려지는 연출

blocks.b:
A 16¼-inch archtop. Carved spruce top, maple back and sides, mahogany neck, rosewood fingerboard, adjustable truss rod.

The magnets and coil sit inside the body. Only a blade shows above the top, running under all six strings rather than a pole piece for each, positioned where the fingerboard ends.

media.note: 픽업 클로즈업(지판 끝에 붙은 위치가 보이게) + 바디 측면. 1937 카탈로그 35쪽 스캔을 보조로

blocks.b:
Charlie Christian played with Benny Goodman from 1939 to 1942. Gibson's history says he "would establish the electric guitar as an instrument with its own unique voice."

Sixty years later, the company writes, the ES-150 is still known as the Charlie Christian model, and some jazz players consider its pickup the best jazz pickup ever made.

Christian died of tuberculosis in 1942, aged 25.

media.note: 찰리 크리스천 사진 + 1939~41년 베니 굿맨 섹스텟 녹음 클립. 사진 저작권 확인 필요

blocks.b:
The model did not stay fixed. Sales slumped by 1940 and the facelift brought new pickups using the then-new Alnico magnets. By 1948 Gibson had introduced its first two-pickup configuration on the ES-150.

Gibson describes the result as a double-edged sword: the ES-150's success established the company as the foremost maker of electric guitars, and at the same time challenged it to top the achievement. Production then broke for the Second World War.

Gibson's catalogue advertised it as "the perfect electric Spanish guitar."

media.note: ES-150_01 — 앰프와 함께 선 전신 사진. changes·impact·coda 병합

blocks.b:
Gibson's history places the ES-175 in what it calls the golden age of innovation — the years after the Second World War, under the aggressive leadership of company president Ted McCarty.

In 1949 Gibson debuted two new concepts: the ES-5, the first three-pickup guitar, and the ES-175, "the first guitar with a sharply pointed cutaway bout."

media.note: 정면 누끼. 후보: Wikimedia 'Gibson 1959 VOS ES-175' CC BY 2.0 1733px (재현품) 또는 'Herb Ellis 1953 Gibson ES-175' CC BY-SA 4.0 2540px

blocks.b:
A top-line archtop before the war was a large instrument. Stromberg's Master 400 measured 19 inches across the lower bout; Epiphone's Emperor 18½; Gibson's own Super 400, 18.

They were hand-carved and expensive, and with a pickup fitted and the amplifier turned up they fed back.

media.note: Gibson Super 400이나 Stromberg Master 400 같은 대형 아치탑 사진. ES-175와 크기를 나란히 비교하는 그래픽으로 만들면 더 좋음

blocks.b:
The ES-175 was Gibson's first archtop built with a laminated maple top rather than a carved solid one. Gibson's own later descriptions of the model list body, top, back and sides all in laminated maple.

Lamination was the cheaper method. It is also stiffer and less lively than a carved top, which is why the guitar resists feedback at volume.

media.note: f홀 안쪽으로 합판 단면과 평행 브레이스가 보이는 사진. 또는 카브드 탑 vs 합판 탑 단면 비교 다이어그램

blocks.b:
Gibson's archtops had used the rounded Venetian cutaway. The ES-175 came with a point.

Its origin is unsettled. Adrian Ingram, who wrote a book on the model, has repeated a claim that a young Kenny Burrell brought Gibson a blonde L-5 fitted with a Charlie Christian pickup and asked for the horn to be cut deeper. Photographs of Burrell with such a guitar exist; documentation connecting it to the design does not.

media.note: 뾰족한 플로렌틴 컷어웨이 클로즈업. 둥근 베네치안 컷어웨이와 나란히 비교하면 차이가 바로 보임

blocks.b:
16¼ inches at the lower bout, 3⅜ inches deep. Mahogany neck joined at the 14th fret, 19 frets, double parallelogram inlays, crown on the headstock.

One dog-ear P-90 at the neck — the pickup Gibson had introduced in 1946. Sunburst, or Natural for more money.

media.note: P-90 도그이어 픽업 클로즈업 + 더블 패럴렐로그램 인레이. 상판에 직접 박힌 토글 스위치도 보이게

blocks.b:
A two-pickup ES-175D followed in the early 1950s. In 1957 the P-90s were replaced by Gibson's new humbuckers. The single-pickup model ran until 1971.

The fittings moved through the usual Gibson sequence — barrel knobs to speed knobs in 1953, bonnets in 1955, reflectors in 1960, witch hats in 1966 — which is how most people date one.

media.note: P-90 → PAF 험버커 교체를 보여주는 두 장 비교. 연도별 노브 변화(배럴 → 스피드 → 보닛 → 리플렉터 → 위치햇) 타임라인 그래픽도 가능

blocks.b:
Herb Ellis, Joe Pass, Jim Hall, Wes Montgomery and Pat Metheny all played the model. Many bought the two-pickup version and used only the neck pickup.

It was not confined to jazz. Steve Howe used one in Yes, and the gold ES-295 Scotty Moore played on the early Elvis records is the same body with different fittings.

media.note: 허브 엘리스 또는 조 패스 연주 사진 + 1950~70년대 재즈 기타 녹음 클립. 라이선스 확인 필요

blocks.b: Pat Metheny removed the bridge pickup and its controls from his ES-175 and taped over the holes. The rest of the instrument records decades of repair: a microphone inside the treble f-hole, replacement tuners, a bound headstock added later, and a toothbrush pushed through the tailpiece in place of a missing strap button.

media.note: 팻 메시니의 실제 기타 사진(테이프로 막은 픽업 구멍, 테일피스의 칫솔이 보이는 컷). 저작권 확인 필요 — 어려우면 일러스트로 재현

blocks.b: Clean late-1950s examples are scarce. Once Les Paul Standards of the same years reached high prices, the 175 became a parts source: its humbuckers, tuners, knobs and switches were pulled to complete conversions of far more valuable guitars.

media.note: PAF 험버커 단품 사진. 또는 '부품이 뜯겨나간' 상태를 보여주는 빈티지 매물 사진

blocks.b: Seventy years in production. Gibson discontinued it, reissued it, and discontinued it again.

media.note: 여백. 다음 챕터(1951 Fender Telecaster)로 전환

credit.en: 3D model: “Fender Custom Shop 1950 Esquire Heavy Relic” by sgab_viz (Sketchfab), CC BY-NC 4.0
credit.ko: 3D 모델: “Fender Custom Shop 1950 Esquire Heavy Relic” — sgab_viz (Sketchfab), CC BY-NC 4.0
credit.ja: 3Dモデル: “Fender Custom Shop 1950 Esquire Heavy Relic” — sgab_viz (Sketchfab), CC BY-NC 4.0

blocks.b:
Fender's own account of why it built this guitar: before 1950 the company had focused on lap steel guitars and amplifiers, and did well at it. But with players like Django Reinhardt, Charlie Christian, T-Bone Walker, Muddy Waters and Big Bill Broonzy increasingly incorporating electric guitars, "it made perfect sense for us to want to have our own version of a 'Spanish style' model on the market."

"And from this necessity, the Broadcaster was born — one of the very first solid-body electric guitars that was built to meet the needs of modern musicians."

Broadcaster was this guitar's first name. By the autumn of 1951 it was the Telecaster.

media.note: 3D 모델(Fender Custom Shop 1950 Esquire Heavy Relic) — 들머리·전체 모습

blocks.b:
The single-pickup Esquire came first in 1950. Fender describes it as a pine body, a bolt-on maple neck, and a lone repurposed lap-steel pickup in the bridge position.

The Broadcaster followed the same year with two — the guitar that would become the Telecaster.

Fender's description of the design: "an efficient, solid-body workhorse with a single cutaway, an intuitive two-pickup configuration, elegant two-knob, three-position switch controls, plus a striking Blonde finish with a black pickguard for contrast."

The neck is one piece of maple with the frets pressed directly into it, and it bolts on with four screws. Strings pass through the body and anchor underneath. The bridge carries three brass saddles for six strings.

media.note: 브리지 플레이트 3새들 클로즈업 + 넥 조인트 나사 4개 + 몸통 뒷면 줄 구멍. 분해 도식으로 '부품의 집합'임을 보여주기

blocks.b:
Leo Fender filed on the bridge and pickup as a single assembly on 13 January 1950, before the guitar had a name. The stated objects read as a manufacturing brief:

"First, to provide a device of this class which is particularly suitable for electrically amplified guitars or similar musical instruments and which incorporates a novel sectional bridge permitting individual adjustment of the strings. Second, to provide a device of this class wherein the pickup unit may be accurately adjusted relative to the strings of the instrument. Third, to provide on the whole, a compact assembly which although economical of manufacture and installation is particularly dependable and effective in operation."

One line accounts for the detail everyone notices: "it has been found desirable to set the pickup unit in acute angular relation with the strings rather than at right angles thereto."

media.note: US2573254 Fig.1~3 — 솔리드 바디, 3분할 새들, 몸통을 관통하는 줄 구멍이 모두 그려져 있음. 퍼블릭 도메인

blocks.b:
"The only problem with it was calling it the 'Broadcaster,' which had already been trademarked by Gretsch."

Fender's solution, in the company's own words: "rather than capitulating and pulling this line of ingenious instruments out of stores and catalogs, we did a quick bit of rebranding. We simply took the 'Broadcaster' label off of the headstock and continued to get our new model into the hands of players."

Those guitars are now called Nocasters.

media.note: 헤드스톡 데칼 비교 3컷: Broadcaster → 이름이 잘려나간 'Nocaster' → Telecaster. 실물 사진 권리 확인 필요

blocks.b:
In 1951 Don Randall, one of Leo Fender's first collaborators, suggested the name Telecaster — televisions were becoming ubiquitous and Fender wanted to attach itself to them.

Fender notes that the rebrand "did not result in nor require any significant changes to the instrument."

The target market was western swing players, whose music was still a dominant form of entertainment in the late 1940s and early 1950s.

By Fender's telling, Leo Fender and George Fullerton took the new guitar out to clubs to let western swing players try it. They presented it to Jimmy Bryant, who took it for a spin during his break and then played it for the rest of the set. "For many, Bryant is considered the original Telecaster adopter."

Jimmy Wyble, Charlie Aldrich, Roy Watkins and Bill Carson followed. Honky-tonk players took it next — Buck Owens, Luther Perkins, James Burton.

Dealers at the trade shows called the new Fender a canoe paddle and a snow shovel.

Fender filed a design patent on the body shape on 23 April 1951. It was granted that August.

media.note: 1950~51년 펜더 광고 또는 NAMM 전시 사진 — 확보 필요. 없으면 디자인 특허 USD164227 도면(PD)으로 대체

blocks.b:
Solid-body electrics existed already — Les Paul's Log around 1941, Paul Bigsby's instrument for Merle Travis in 1948 — but as single pieces made by hand for one player.

The Telecaster was drawn to be produced in quantity from parts that bolt together. It is still made to substantially the same drawing.

media.note: 1952 Les Paul Goldtop · 1954 Stratocaster 챕터 링크 카드. 생산 라인 사진이 있으면 좋음
